scenes.title: Key ideas
items: Money is a record of who owns what
A blockchain is a ledger that thousands of computers keep a copy of and agree on together
A cryptocurrency is a unit recorded on a blockchain
A smart contract is a program that lives on a blockchain and follows fixed rules, for…
Stablecoins are tokens designed to stay worth $1 (e.g. USDC, USDT)
scenes.vo: First, money is a record of who owns what. Your bank balance is a line in your bank's private ledger (record book). You trust the bank to keep it correct. Next, A blockchain is a ledger that thousands of computers keep a copy of and agree on together. New entries are added in batches called blocks, each linked to the one before: a chain of blocks. Nobody can quietly change an old entry, because everyone else's copy would disagree. Then, A cryptocurrency is a unit recorded on a blockchain. Bitcoin (bitcoin) was the first (2009). Ether (ETH) is the currency of the Ethereum blockchain, which also runs programs. Also, A smart contract is a program that lives on a blockchain and follows fixed rules, for example "whoever deposits X gets Y back plus interest". On top of that, Stablecoins are tokens designed to stay worth $1 (for example U.S.D.C., U.S.D.T.). You'll use them a lot, but they can fail (Lesson 1.5).

scenes.title: Key ideas (cont.)
items: DeFi (decentralised finance) is financial services (trading, lending, earning interest)…
scenes.vo: And DeFi (decentralised finance) is financial services (trading, lending, earning interest) run by smart contracts instead of banks. And finally, the trade-off: no bank in the middle means nobody can freeze your money, but also nobody can reverse your mistakes. That's why this program starts with safety.

scenes.title: Worked example
steps: When Alice sends Bob 0.1 ETH, she doesn't send a file.
She signs an instruction ("move 0.1 ETH from my address to Bob's").
The network checks she owns it, adds it to the next block, and every copy of…
scenes.vo: Let's work an example, step by step. When Alice sends Bob 0.1 ETH, she doesn't send a file. She signs an instruction ("move 0.1 ETH from my address to Bob's"). The network checks she owns it, adds it to the next block, and every copy of the ledger updates. Bob now owns it. There is no "undo" button.

scenes.q: Why can't someone quietly change an old blockchain entry?
scenes.a: Thousands of computers hold copies and would reject a version that doesn't match.
scenes.vo: Question one. Why can't someone quietly change an old blockchain entry? [[pause 4]] The answer: Thousands of computers hold copies and would reject a version that doesn't match.

scenes.q: What is a stablecoin designed to do?
scenes.a: Stay worth about $1 (or another currency). It can still fail.
scenes.vo: Question two. What is a stablecoin designed to do? [[pause 4]] The answer: Stay worth about $1 (or another currency). It can still fail.

scenes.q: What does DeFi replace, and what do you give up?
scenes.a: It replaces banks and brokers with smart contracts. You give up anyone who can reverse mistakes or help recover funds.
